title: How Stephen Miller Schemed His Way to the Top
gist: After Republicans lost both the House and the Senate in the midterms, Trump named Stephen Miller White House chief of staff in place of Susie Wiles, apparently prizing loyalty ahead of the congressional investigations expected next year. The text reports the appointment and the personnel fallout rather than the 'scheming' the title suggests; more firings (Blair, Walters) are expected, and Hegseth's position is strengthened.

insights.claim: Republicans lost both the House and the Senate in the midterms, the worst GOP midterm performance in decades, and Trump privately blamed chief of staff Susie Wiles, who resigned.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Divided government means legislative gridlock and an investigation-heavy Congress from next year.
insights.quote: less than a week after Republicans lost the House and Senate in a searing rebuke of Trump’s policy agenda

insights.claim: Trump named Stephen Miller, the architect of the second term's immigration crackdown, as chief of staff from Monday, choosing him over Steve Witkoff and Jay Clayton.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Choosing a hardliner signals policy escalation rather than moderation after the electoral defeat.

insights.claim: Trump apparently chose Miller because of his zeal in defending the president and his deep loyalty, with congressional investigations looming next year.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: The White House is gearing up for confrontation with a Democratic Congress, so expect more political volatility.
insights.quote: with the looming threat of congressional investigations starting next year

insights.claim: Wiles' deputies James Blair, who designed the GOP midterm strategy, and Richard Walters are seen as vulnerable to being fired by Miller unless they resign first.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: More turnover means less predictable policy.
insights.locator: With Wiles' departure, White House aides

insights.claim: Defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who is ideologically aligned with Miller and had a strained relationship with Wiles, is likely to benefit from the change.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: A Miller-Hegseth axis points to continued aggressive military and security action.

insights.claim: Miller, who also leads the Homeland Security Council, orchestrated last year's campaign of strikes on boats around Venezuela through the Pentagon, working closely with Hegseth.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Raises the odds of further escalation toward Venezuela, a geopolitical risk for oil markets.

insights.claim: Wiles was arguably Trump's most successful chief of staff, after he cycled through chiefs in his first term, so her exit ends a period of relative stability in the West Wing.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: A return to first-term-style churn would add to policy unpredictability.
